lead: The same four blocks — sensor, network, cloud and actuator — appear in a farm, shop, truck, substation and river. What changes is the constraint: a soil probe must run two years on one cell; a cold-chain box must alarm within minutes; a meter must bill a household. Domain-specific IoT fits sensor, radio, interval and power to that constraint. Judge a case study by how it meets the constraint and how it fails, not by sensor count.
prereq: Prerequisites: sensors and actuators (Unit 2), protocol families with payload, range and duty-cycle limits (Unit 3), and cloud analytics with security as a deployment constraint (Unit 5). Protocol detail is not repeated.

blocks.text: Every deployment has four blocks: a sensor that measures, a network that carries the reading, a cloud service that stores and compares, and an actuator or person who acts. The blocks do not change from farm to substation. The constraint that chooses each block does.

A soil probe may sit 2 km from the gateway and must run two years on one cell. A cold-chain box on a fish truck must alarm within 5 minutes of crossing 4 °C. A meter reports every 15 minutes for billing and outage detection. A fitness band must last a day and reach a phone within 10 m.
Read each case backwards. Interval and message size give the data rate; rate and range give the radio; radio and battery give the power budget.

blocks.where: R is the mean bit rate in bit/s; N is the number of messages in the period; S is the message size in bytes; 8 converts bytes to bits; T is the period in seconds.

blocks.text: In agriculture a capacitive soil-moisture probe reports volumetric water content in percent. The node sends every 10 minutes through a field gateway to the cloud. If the value stays below the crop threshold for several readings, the cloud opens a valve. Need-based irrigation saves water and pump current. The same chain is described for water systems in remote monitoring and water management.

A portable wireless interactive sensor is a handheld unit with its own radio. It joins the field network on demand, shows the reading and can switch a valve from where the farmer stands. It covers patches with no fixed node.

In retail, a shelf weight mat or infrared beam detects a gap and creates a refill task. A chiller logger alarms above its limit. An RFID reader counts cartons at the stockroom door, and electronic shelf labels update prices from the same cloud.

Logistics repeats this at larger scale: GPS plus cellular modem in each truck, RFID scans at hubs, geofence alarms when a truck leaves its route, and a door sensor for unexpected opening. Parcel scans give the customer the same event the depot sees.

In energy, a smart meter reports every 15 minutes and sends a last-gasp message when supply is lost, so the utility learns of an outage before the first phone call. At peak load a load-control actuator sheds water heaters and air conditioners for 30 minutes, and the customer is credited for the energy not consumed (the shed kWh). This closed loop is covered in industrial IoT, applied to a grid instead of a plant.

Environment nodes use optical PM2.5, gas carbon-monoxide and ultrasonic water-level sensors. Calibration drift is the main failure: a cheap gas sensor walks away over months, so the node is co-located with a reference or swapped on schedule. Air-quality nodes are dense because pollution varies street by street, unlike a smart city parking bay whose state is local and simple.

Wearables measure optical heart rate, blood oxygen and steps. The band uses Bluetooth Low Energy to a phone, and the phone forwards to the cloud. Battery and skin contact limit it; consent is the deployment constraint. Vehicles combine GPS, OBD-II and an accelerometer for harsh braking. Live tracking needs 4G, a daily summary fits NB-IoT, and a truck that leaves terrestrial coverage needs satellite backhaul.

sections.h3: Judging a case study in seven questions

blocks.text: A case-study answer that lists sensors earns few marks. Run seven questions.

items: State the problem and decision: irrigate, refill or shed load?
List each sensor, what it measures, range and accuracy.
Choose the network from range, payload and duty cycle.
Compute data rate from message size and interval.
Compute power budget: average current × time, compared with cell mAh.
Estimate cost per node and per year in rupees, including SIM or gateway share.
Name the most likely failure mode and how the system detects it.

blocks.text: Many sites over months produce more data than a person can read, so rules and dashboards matter. A dashboard compares 40 farms on one axis; an alarm fires only when a value crosses a limit. Big-data work stores raw series, computes summaries per site per day and ranks sites by water saved.

Security is a constraint. A node must authenticate before its reading is accepted. Meter aggregation must hide one household's daily curve while giving the utility the transformer total. A wearable needs informed consent and a delete path.

figure.caption: Three of the domains are shown; each reuses the same sensor–network–cloud chain and ends in one device.

spec.aria: A tree with root IoT domains branching into agriculture, logistics and energy, each ending in its main device: soil moisture, vehicle tracking and smart meter.

examples.question: A farm deploys 500 soil-moisture sensor nodes. Each node sends one message of 80 bytes every 10 minutes. (a) How many messages does one node send per day? (b) How many messages does the farm send per day? (c) What is the daily data volume in bytes and in MB, taking 1 MB = 10⁶ bytes? (d) What mean bit rate does this need? (e) In EU868/IN865 at the common data rates the LoRaWAN application payload limit is 51 bytes; it depends on region and data rate. How many frames does one reading need, and how many frames per day does the farm send?
steps: One day is 24 × 60 = 1440 minutes. Messages per node per day = 1440 ÷ 10 = 144.
Farm total per day = 500 nodes × 144 messages = 72,000 messages.

In EU868/IN865 at the common data rates the maximum application payload is 51 bytes; it depends on region and data rate. Each 80-byte reading must be split: 80 ÷ 51 = 1.57, so ⌈1.57⌉ = 2 frames per reading.
examples.answer: 144 messages per node per day; 72,000 messages, 5,760,000 bytes (5.76 MB) and a mean rate of 533.33 bit/s for the farm; and 2 frames per reading, that is 144,000 frames per day, because at these settings 80 bytes exceeds the 51-byte payload limit.
examples.check:
import math
n = 500
size = 80
interval = 10
per_node = 24 * 60 // interval
total = n * per_node
bytes_day = total * size
mb_day = bytes_day / 1e6
rate = bytes_day * 8 / 86400
frames = math.ceil(size / 51)
print(per_node)
print(total)
print(bytes_day)
print(round(mb_day, 2))
print(round(rate, 2))
print(frames)
print(frames * total)

traps: Sizing a link from the number of sensors alone. Use message size × interval to get bit/s, then check range and duty cycle.

Reading a payload limit as a frame size. In EU868/IN865 at common data rates the 51-byte LoRaWAN limit is the application payload; headers and MAC commands sit outside it. Other regions and data rates allow larger payloads.
Mixing MB and MiB. 5,760,000 bytes is 5.76 MB in base 10 but about 5.49 MiB in base 2. State the base you used.
Treating a fitness band as a medical device. A band sampling at 1 sample/s is not an ECG at 250 samples/s; the rate and the power budget differ by orders of magnitude.
Describing a case study as a sensor list. Marks come from the constraint, the rate calculation and the named failure mode.

quiz.q: Name three IoT application domains and one device used in each.
quiz.a: Agriculture — soil-moisture node; logistics — GPS vehicle tracker; energy — smart meter. Any three correct pairs earn full marks.

quiz.q: Why can a network not be sized from the number of sensors alone?
quiz.a: The load depends on how much data each sensor sends and how often. Rate follows N × S × 8 ÷ T; 500 nodes sending 80 bytes every 10 minutes need only about 533 bit/s, while 2 cameras need far more.

quiz.q: 200 sensors each send 40 bytes every 15 minutes. Find the messages per day, the bytes per day and the rate in bit/s.
quiz.a: 1440 ÷ 15 = 96 messages per sensor per day. 200 × 96 = 19,200 messages. 19,200 × 40 = 768,000 bytes per day = 0.768 MB. Rate = 768,000 × 8 ÷ 86,400 = 71.11 bit/s.

quiz.q: A cold-chain box must alarm within 5 minutes but runs on a coin cell for a year. What do you change, and what do you lose?
quiz.a: Keep a short interval but cut the payload to a few bytes and use an event-driven rule: send only when the temperature crosses the limit or on a 30-minute heartbeat. The radio sleeps between sends, so the average current fits a coin cell. What is lost is the full temperature history between events, so the device must log locally and upload the log at the depot.

quiz.q: What extra ability does a portable wireless interactive sensor give a farmer over a fixed node?
quiz.a: It joins the field network on demand and shows the reading at the spot, and it can switch a valve from the field. It covers patches with no fixed node and needs no dashboard.

quiz.q: Why is calibration drift a bigger problem for an air-quality node than for a soil-moisture node?
quiz.a: Pollutant levels are compared across sites and against health limits, so a slow offset changes the conclusion. Soil moisture is used against a local threshold for one field: a constant offset only shifts the local threshold slightly, which the farmer absorbs by adjusting the trigger value; absolute accuracy matters less.

quiz.q: What is the LoRaWAN application payload limit, and what does it force when a reading is larger?
quiz.a: In EU868/IN865 at the common data rates the maximum application payload is 51 bytes; it depends on region and data rate. A larger reading must be split into frames, compressed, or sent over a link with a larger payload such as NB-IoT.

beyond: Not for the exam. Tiny machine learning puts a small anomaly detector on the node, so the radio sends an alarm instead of a raw series, cutting the power budget. Satellite IoT backhaul reaches trucks and fields outside terrestrial coverage; eSIM profiles handle roaming. Regulators are pushing product passports that carry battery or device history in a scannable code, making provenance and consent practical case-study questions. Worth searching: 'LoRaWAN payload size', 'TinyML anomaly detection', 'cold chain excursion alarm', 'NB-IoT power saving mode'.
